quiz.question: Where does the majority of the world's population live?

headline: Six Out of Ten Humans Live on One Continent — and It's Not the One You Think
teaser: Close your eyes and picture where the world's people live. You have a mental map -- everyone does -- and it was assembled over years from news coverage, geography lessons, and the general ambient information that seeps in through cultural osmosis. The trouble is, that mental map is almost certainly wrong in a fundamental way. Not wrong about the margins or the details, but wrong about the basic shape of humanity's distribution across the planet. A majority of people, when asked which continent holds the most humans, confidently choose the wrong one. This is not a trick question. It is a straightforward one that reveals something fascinating about the gap between the world as it is and the world as we imagine it.
metaDescription: About 60% of all people — 4.7 billion — live in Asia. 58% of survey respondents get this wrong, most guessing Africa.
summary: If you were to gather every human being on Earth into a single queue — an enterprise that would stretch roughly to Mars and cause unimaginable problems for catering — about six out of every ten people in that queue would be Asian. Asia is home to approximately 4.7 billion people, which is more than Africa, Europe, and the Americas combined. This has been the case for centuries, and yet a majority of people surveyed guess incorrectly, most commonly selecting Africa, which currently holds about 18%.
nuance: Asia's share is expected to decline slowly over the coming decades as population growth shifts to sub-Saharan Africa. By 2100, under median UN projections, Africa's share could rise from 18% to over 35%, while Asia's could fall to around 45%. China and India alone account for roughly 35% of all humans today, but China's population is already shrinking. The mental map most people carry — shaped by news coverage of African population growth — has leapt ahead of where the numbers actually are right now.
aside: It is a peculiar feature of the human mind that we can know, in a vague sort of way, that China and India each contain over a billion people, and yet still be startled to learn that most humans are Asian. It is as if we store facts about continents in a different mental filing cabinet from facts about countries, and the two cabinets do not communicate.

emailDigestLine: Six in ten humans live on a single continent, and most people guess the wrong one.
premiumTeaser: Why does almost everyone get this wrong? The answer involves a peculiar collision between colonial-era cartography, the Mercator projection, and the way television news selects its establishing shots — a set of biases so deeply embedded that even people who know the data still feel surprised by it.
b2bClassroomNote: Classroom discussion: Have students draw a pie chart of world population by continent before revealing the actual figures. Connects to SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities) and introduces demographic transition theory.
publishingNote: UN WPP and OWID data closely aligned. Nuance addresses the coming demographic shift to Africa honestly.
